analysis.one_liner: Makes beverage, packaging, and plastic producers pay for and reduce single-use plastic waste.
analysis.headline: Introduced in October 2023, the bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the same day and never received a hearing or vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would shift the cost of single-use plastic waste from taxpayers and local governments to the companies that make and sell plastic packaging. Producers would have to join industry-funded organizations that pay for collecting, recycling, and reusing packaging, meet plastic source-reduction targets, use minimum levels of recycled material, and remove certain toxic chemicals from beverage containers. It would also create a national 10-cent refundable deposit on beverage containers, set limits on plastic-pellet pollution from plastics plants, and add environmental justice protections for communities near those facilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who live near plastics plants, drink from beverage containers, and pay local taxes for waste pickup and litter cleanup. Communities near plastic production facilities get environmental justice protections and tighter discharge limits on plastic pellets. Consumers get a nationwide 10-cent refundable deposit on bottles and cans, safer packaging with certain toxic chemicals removed, and a funding stream that takes recycling and cleanup costs off local property taxes. The recycling and composting industry gets producer money to build out collection and reprocessing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near plastics plants and local taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Producers of packaging, food service products, and beverage containers must join Producer Responsibility Organizations, pay membership fees, and fully fund the collection, reuse, recycling, and composting system for their products, with recycling rate targets of at least 50% by 2030 and 65% by 2040.

A national beverage container deposit program requires retailers to charge consumers a deposit of at least 10 cents at purchase and refund it when the empty container is returned, with producers funding redemption centers open to the public.

Single-use plastic must be cut 25% by weight by 2032 and 50% by 2050 versus a 2024 baseline, and by January 2033 all covered products and beverage containers must be reusable, recyclable, or compostable.

Plastic beverage containers must contain rising minimum levels of post-consumer recycled material, starting at 15% by 2025 and reaching 60% by 2040, and retailers are barred from selling single-use PET beverage containers that are opaque or pigmented or that contain toxic substances such as PFAS, phthalates, and bisphenols.

The bill excludes incineration, pyrolysis, gasification, and other chemical conversion processes from counting as recycling, sets effluent limits on wastewater and runoff carrying plastic pellets from polymer production and molding facilities, and directs environmental justice protections at covered facilities, including fair treatment for census tracts with higher shares of people of color and low-income households.
A Reduction and Litter Cleanup Trust Fund is established in the Treasury, funded in part by resin makers, to pay for litter cleanup and pollution mitigation.

analysis.who_pays: Plastic resin makers, consumer packaged goods and beverage companies, and packaging producers, who must fund the collection system, meet reduction and recycled-content targets, pay trust fund fees, and redesign packaging. Retailers bear the work of collecting and refunding containers. Producers are barred from charging these fees as a separate line on a receipt, so the costs would arrive embedded in product prices, and consumers pay a refundable deposit on every covered beverage at purchase.

drawbacks.text: Although producers cannot pass the program fees to consumers as a separate item on a receipt, the money still has to come from somewhere, so the costs would surface in higher prices on packaged goods and drinks.
Every covered beverage purchase includes a deposit of at least 10 cents, raising the up-front price at the register; consumers get it back only if they return the container.

The Producer Responsibility Organizations that run the new system are governed by boards made up of the producers themselves, which hands the industry control over how the recycling money is spent, with oversight from EPA-approved advisory committees that include recyclers, local governments, environmental groups, and tribes.

A good-faith objection supporters would acknowledge: the compliance timelines begin quickly (recycled-content rules by January 2025, organization plans by August 2025), which could be difficult for supply chains to meet, and the small-producer exemption (under $1 million in annual revenue or under 1 ton of products) means a meaningful slice of the market would not contribute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: consumers would pay somewhat more for packaged goods and deposits up front, but in exchange producers rather than local taxpayers fund recycling and litter cleanup, toxic chemicals come out of beverage containers, and plastics production itself must shrink over decades. The main design weakness is that the producers pay the bills and also control the boards of the organizations that spend them, so enforcement and ambition depend heavily on EPA audits and advisory committee oversight. On balance the costs are visible and moderate while the benefits, cleaner waterways, safer packaging, and lower municipal waste burdens, are broad and long-lived.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never scheduled a hearing or vote, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on October 25, 2023 with 11 original cosponsors, all Democrats or the Independent Sen. Sanders.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction; that is the last action recorded.
No further action, hearing, markup, or vote was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill lapsed with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Plastic resin makers and beverage and consumer goods companies are better off: they avoid the producer fees, deposit funding, recycled-content mandates, and source-reduction targets the bill would have imposed. Local governments and taxpayers continue to absorb the costs of managing and cleaning up plastic waste.

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Break Free From Plastic Pollution Act of 2023 in the Senate on October 25, 2023.

for.name: Environmental and anti-plastic-pollution advocacy organizations
for.what_they_did: Publicly championed the Break Free From Plastic Pollution Act and pushed for its introduction and passage.

against.name: Tom Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on October 25, 2023 and never scheduled a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Plastics and petrochemical industry trade groups, including the American Chemistry Council
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Break Free From Plastic Pollution Act and lobbied against producer-responsibility mandates, deposit programs, and restrictions on plastics production.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 initial sponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sen. Sanders, with no Republican support, and the bill never reached the floor of either chamber.

industries.note: The bill imposes source-reduction targets on plastic, mandates rising recycled content, bans toxic substances, sets effluent limits on plastic-pellet pollution from their plants, requires trust fund payments from resin makers, and excludes chemical recycling outputs from counting as recycling. Companies that profit from selling more virgin plastic would face shrinking demand and new compliance costs.

industries.industry: Consumer packaged goods and beverage companies
industries.note: They must fund the entire collection, recycling, and reuse system for their packaging through producer fees, run a national bottle-deposit program, and redesign packaging to be reusable, recyclable, or compostable by 2033. Today those cleanup costs fall on municipalities and taxpayers, so the bill moves a burden they currently avoid back onto their own books.

Retailers must accept returned containers and pay refunds regardless of brand for stores over 5,000 square feet, and are barred from selling certain pigmented or toxic-laden beverage containers. It is a compliance burden, but the refund goes back to their customers.

industries.industry: Recycling, composting, and waste collection industries
industries.note: Producer fees must fund collection service providers, recyclers, composters, and development of end markets for recycled materials, including payments negotiated with curbside programs. This is the industry that would receive the new funding stream.

The bill's definition of recycling excludes incineration, pyrolysis, gasification, and similar chemical conversion, so these operations cannot count toward the bill's targets or access its funding. Their interest in being treated as recyclers runs against the bill's goal of preserving material quality.
